title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F30
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 37 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.label: Cross-agent Synthesis
items.question: Find out what the ESA Science Strategy says about solid Earth deformation and land subsidence in urban environments, then search arXiv for recent papers on InSAR-based urban subsidence or land deformation monitoring from satellite data. Compare the scale and focus of the research literature with the strategy's urban deformation monitoring objectives — identify what the community is actively pursuing versus what the strategy emphasises.

answers.text:
The ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy (EOSS) knowledge graph does not directly provide bibliographic details or research papers. However, I can guide you on how to interpret the strategy's likely emphasis on solid Earth deformation and land subsidence in urban environments based on ESA's mission priorities and thematic focus areas.

For the arXiv search, here are 5 recent papers (2020–2024) on InSAR-based urban subsidence or land deformation monitoring using satellite data. These papers focus on methods, case studies, and technological advancements in the field:

1. Forecasting landslides using community detection on geophysical satellite data (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.12038v2)
   • Authors: Vrinda Desai, Farnaz Fazelpour, Alexander L. Handwerger, Karen E. Daniels
   • Published: 2022-12-22
   • Key Focus:
     • Uses InSAR data to detect pre-failure deformation in landslides.
     • Applies multilayer modularity optimization to identify clusters of ground deformation.
     • Demonstrates community persistence as a metric for predicting catastrophic failure.
   • Link: PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.12038v2)

2. Remote estimation of geologic composition using interferometric synthetic-aperture radar in California's Central Valley (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.04813v1)
   • Authors: Kyongsik Yun, Kyra Adams, John Reager, Zhen Liu, Caitlyn Chavez, Michael Turmon, Thomas Lu
   • Published: 2022-12-04
   • Key Focus:
     • Investigates land subsidence in California's Central Valley due to groundwater pumping.
     • Uses InSAR-based deformation data to estimate geologic composition via machine learning (random forest and deep neural networks).
     • Achieves high accuracy even with sparse sampling, suggesting generalizability to other regions.
   • Link: PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.04813v1)

3. Monitoring surface deformation over oilfield using MT-InSAR and production well data (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.10985v1)
   • Authors: Sarah Narges Fatholahi, Hongjie He, Lanying Wang, Awase Syed, Jonathan Li
   • Published: 2021-03-18
   • Key Focus:
     • Uses Small BAseline Subset (SBAS) InSAR to monitor surface deformation in an oilfield in Iran.
     • Compares InSAR results with oil production rates to assess the impact of petroleum extraction.
     • Identifies maximum subsidence of 13.5 mm/year due to tectonic and non-tectonic factors.
   • Link: PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.10985v1)

4. Bayesian Poroelastic Aquifer Characterization from InSAR Surface Deformation Data Part II: Quantifying the Uncertainty (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.04577v1)
   • Authors: Amal Alghamdi, Marc Hesse, Jingyi Chen, Umberto Villa, Omar Ghattas
   • Published: 2021-02-08
   • Key Focus:
     • Develops a Bayesian inversion framework to quantify uncertainty in groundwater aquifer parameters using InSAR deformation data.
     • Uses generalized preconditioned Crank–Nicolson (gpCN) MCMC for scalable uncertainty quantification.
     • Demonstrates applicability in a real-world aquifer test in Nevada.
   • Link: PDF (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.04577v1)

5. Bayesian Poroelastic Aquifer Characterization from InSAR Surface Deformation Data. Part I: Maximum A Posteriori Estimate (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.10706v1)
   • Authors: Amal Alghamdi, Marc A. Hesse, Jingyi Chen, Omar Ghattas
   • Published: 2020-02

items.question: Find the CDS dataset for downloading Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI atmospheric composition data.

answers.text: I currently don't have the tools to directly find the CDS dataset for downloading Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI atmospheric composition data. However, you can typically access this data through the Copernicus Open Access Hub or the Copernicus Climate Data Store.

The CDSE agent provided information about Sentinel-5P TROPOMI data availability via the Sentinel Hub API on CDSE, listing available trace gas products and offering to fetch imagery if given a location and date range. This directly answers the user's question about finding the dataset and explains how to access it. I will return this result directly as instructed.

Here are the relevant CDS (Copernicus Data Space) datasets and methods for downloading Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI atmospheric composition data:

1. Sentinel-5P L2 Products via CDSE (Sentinel Hub)
• Collection: Sentinel-5P L2 (Level 2) products
• Data Types: Trace gases, aerosols, and cloud data (e.g., NO₂, CO, O₃, SO₂, CH₄, HCHO, aerosol index, cloud fraction).
• Access Methods:
  • Sentinel Hub API (via CDSE):
    Use the fetch_sentinel5p_l2 tool with parameters like:

    fetch_sentinel5p_l2(
        bbox=[west, south, east, north],  # Bounding box (e.g., [10, 40, 15, 45])
        start_date="YYYY-MM-DD",          # Start date
        end_date="YYYY-MM-DD",            # End date
        preset="no2",                     # Preset for the product (e.g., "no2", "co", "o3", "so2", "ch4", "hcho", "aer_ai_340_380", "cloud_fraction")
        as_geotiff=True                   # For quantitative analysis (raw FLOAT32 values)
    )

  • CDSE Web Interface:
    Visit Copernicus Data Space Environment (https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/) and search for Sentinel-5P L2 products.
  • API Access:
    Use the Copernicus Open Access Hub API or Sentinel Hub API for programmatic queries.

2. STAC Collections (EO Dashboards)
For metadata and discovery, the following STAC collections are available:
• N1_NO2 (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/NO2_daily/collection.json) (Daily NO₂ data)
• N1_CH4 (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/methane_monitoring/collection.json) (Methane monitoring)
• N1_CO (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/CO_3_daily/collection.json) (Daily CO data)
• N1_SO2 (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/so2_daily/collection.json) (Daily SO₂ data)
• N1_NO2_jaxa (https://esa-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-catalog/trilateral/N1_NO2_jaxa/collection.json) (NO₂ data processed by JAXA)

These collections provide metadata and STAC items for discovery but do not directly host downloadable files. Use them to identify time ranges, bounding boxes, or specific products before downloading via CDSE.

3. Key Notes
• Sentinel-5P L2 products are geophysical values (e.g., mol/m², DU) and require as_geotiff=True for quantitative analysis.
• Presets like no2, co, etc., are optimized for visualization or analysis.
• For custom requests (e.g., specific dates, regions, or products), provide:
  • A place name or coordinates.
  • A date range.
  • The specific product (e.g., NO₂, CO, CH₄).

To download Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI atmospheric composition data via the CDSE, you can use the fetch_sentinel5p_l2 tool.

Depending on the specific atmospheric component you are interested in, you can use the following preset options:

• no2: Nitrogen Dioxide
• co: Carbon Monoxide
• o3: Ozone
• so2: Sulphur Dioxide
• ch4: Methane
• hcho: Formaldehyde
• aer_ai_340_380: Aerosol Index
• cloud_fraction: Cloud Fraction

Usage Note:
• For a visual overview, the tool returns a JPEG by default.
• For quantitative analysis (e.g., physical values in $\text{mol/m}^2$), set as_geotiff=True to receive a georeferenced GeoTIFF containing the raw $\text{FLOAT32}$ data.

Here are the relevant CDS (Copernicus Data Space) datasets and methods for downloading Copernicus Sentinel-5P TROPOMI atmospheric composition data:

  • CDSE Web Interface:

3. Key Notes

2. Direct Download (Browser Access)
Use the CDSE Browser for manual downloads:

Steps:
1. Navigate to:

2. Select the product type (e.g., L2NO2_, L2O3, L2CO, L2CH4_, L2SO2_, L2AER_AI, L2CLOUD_).
3. Filter by date, area (bbox), or cloud cover.
4. Click the download icon (⤓) to get the full product (NetCDF format).

3. Product Types (Sentinel-5P TROPOMI)
Product       | Product Type | DescriptionNO₂               | L2NO2_     | Nitrogen Dioxide
O₃                | L2O3     | Ozone

4. Programmatic Access (Python Example)
Use the CDSE STAC API for automated downloads:

import pystac_client

Open the STAC API
catalog = pystac_client.Client.open("https://catalogue.dataspace.copernicus.eu/stac/")

Search for Sentinel-5P NO₂ data
search = catalog.search(
    collections=["sentinel-5p-l2"],
    bbox=[2, 49, 16, 55],  # Example: Germany
    datetime="2024-01-01/2024-01-02",
    query={"s5p:product_type": {"eq": "L2NO2_"}}
)

Download the first result
items = list(search.items())
if items:
    print(f"Download URL: {items[0].assets['download'].href}")

5. Alternative Access

  (Note: This is being phased out in favor of CDSE.)

items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for narratives about wildfires, then find a MOOC lecture that teaches the satellite techniques used to detect and monitor active fires from space.

answers.text:
The EO Dashboard contains a narrative on the Australian bushfires of 2019-2020, which demonstrates the use of the TROPOMI instrument on Sentinel-5P to monitor carbon monoxide (CO) levels as a proxy for estimating CO2 emissions from wildfires.

Regarding educational materials, the MOOC lecture "Fire Monitoring: Fire monitoring with Remote Sensing" covers the following techniques:
• Active Fire Detection: Using platforms like FIRMS (NASA MODIS, NASA VIIRS, NOAA Suomi NPP) and EFIS, which utilize mid-infrared radiation emissions and cloud mass testing to detect active fires.
• Burn Severity Monitoring: Using the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR), which compares pre- and post-fire imagery using near-infrared and shortwave infrared bands to assess vegetation damage.

Here is what I found:

EO Dashboard Narratives on Wildfires
The EO Dashboard narrative about wildfires discusses the 2019-2020 Australian bushfires, emphasizing their significant environmental impact, including the emission of 700 million metric tons of CO2. It highlights the role of satellite data, particularly from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P mission's TROPOMI instrument, in accurately measuring emissions and understanding the connection between wildfires and climate change.

MOOC Lecture on Satellite Techniques for Detecting and Monitoring Active Fires
Here are the relevant MOOC lecture chunks that teach satellite techniques for detecting and monitoring active fires from space:

[1] Fire Monitoring: Fire monitoring with Remote Sensing
Source: Fire Monitoring - Introduction

Content:
• Learning Goals:
  • Understand how remote sensing supports fire monitoring.
  • Distinguish between fire intensity (during a fire) and fire severity (after a fire).
  • Learn how to monitor fire burn severity using remote sensing data.

• Key Concepts:
  • Fire Triangle: Oxygen, heat, and fuel are essential for a fire to exist.
  • Fire Intensity: Energy released during a fire (e.g., temperature, duration, radiation power).
  • Fire Severity: Post-fire assessment of organic matter loss (above and below ground).

• Role of Earth Observation:
  • Prevention: Monitor hazard conditions (e.g., high temperatures, dry vegetation) and map risk areas.
  • Active Fires: Detect emissions (smoke), measure temperatures, and track fire size and direction.
  • Post-Fire: Monitor burned vegetation, soil, and vegetation recovery.

• Remote Sensing Techniques:
  • Spectral Response: Vegetation reflects differently in the near-infrared (NIR) and shortwave infrared (SWIR) bands compared to burned areas.
  • Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR): Uses NIR and SWIR bands to assess burn severity (high/medium/low severity).
